column3: It is the closest counterpart, extending the focus's inability to escape on earth to heaven while repeating the denial of any protector or helper apart from God.

It repeats the denial of any protector or helper apart from God and grounds it in His dominion over heaven and earth.
It pairs the same denial of protector and helper with God's ownership of heaven and earth, though the central wording is already established.
Within the same passage it states that disputants have no escape, directly sharpening the focus's inescapability.
It confirms the promised event as true and says its hearers cannot thwart it, adding certainty to the focus's warning.
It joins inability to escape on earth with having no protectors besides God, while locating the consequence in multiplied punishment.
Its rule concerning response after wrongdoing does not clarify escape from God or the absence of divine alternatives.
It repeats that disbelievers cannot escape on earth but adds only their destination in the Fire after earlier direct parallels.
It links the arrival of the threatened matter to God's will and denies the hearers any power to thwart it.

Its rule of proportionate retaliation and forgiveness does not add to the focus's themes.

It denies alleged partners any possession, share, or supporting role in heaven and earth, reinforcing the lack of alternatives to God.
Its description of prayer, consultation, and spending does not clarify the focus's warning.
Its assurance that God's servants receive help is a narrow positive counterpart to the focus's denial of other help.
Its rebuke for unjust exultation on earth does not add to inescapability or protection.

It applies the absence of any protector or helper besides God to unavoidable recompense for wrongdoing.

Lordship over heaven and earth supplies only general sovereignty context.

Its prediction of a military reversal in a nearby land does not clarify the focus.

Its promise of help in battle does not explain the focus's exclusive divine protection.

Its command to prepare military force does not clarify the focus's claim.

It links worship without authority or knowledge to the wrongdoers' lack of a helper.

Its statement about alliances among disbelievers concerns communal relations rather than divine protection.

Its prohibition on taking unbelieving relatives as allies concerns communal loyalty, not rescue from God.

Its description of spreading and planting the earth does not clarify the focus.

Its account of night and day as mercy does not develop the focus.

Its household etiquette and marriage prohibition do not clarify the focus.

Its prohibition on despairing of God's mercy does not clarify escape or protection.

It states that no one can overcome those God helps and no one can help those He forsakes, directly clarifying exclusive aid.
It names God as sufficient both as Protector and as Helper, the positive counterpart to the focus's denial of either apart from Him.

It challenges invoking besides God what can neither harm nor benefit, undermining reliance on any alternative source of protection.

It warns of gathering before God where people have no protector or intercessor apart from Him.
It identifies God as the true Protector and contrasts His guardianship with all false objects of reliance.
It affirms that nothing befalls believers except what God has decreed and names Him their Protector.
It presents God as sufficient and the sole object of reliance, supplying the faithful response to the focus's denial of alternatives.
It says no one can remove harm God wills or withhold His bounty, directly depicting His unmatched control.
It says that when God wills harm for a people none can repel it and they have no protector apart from Him.
It challenges the taking of protectors besides God who lack power over benefit or harm.
It observes that when harm touches people they call on God alone, showing where help is actually sought in need.
It denies that those invoked besides God control provision or possess any power, excluding them as viable helpers.
It challenges those invoked besides God as unable to remove harm or alter it.
It says that one whom God leaves astray will never find protectors apart from Him.
It denies that anyone whom God leaves astray can find a guiding protector.
It asks who could protect people from the Merciful and says their alleged gods cannot help even themselves or be protected from Him.
It depicts God as the one who protects while none can be protected against Him, a direct formulation of unilateral divine power.
It denies that alleged gods control harm, benefit, death, life, or resurrection, exposing their inability to provide rescue.
It commands reliance on God and declares Him sufficient as guardian, the positive response to the focus's warning.
It says no one can withhold the mercy God releases or release what He withholds, directly expressing unopposable divine action.
It says that if the Merciful intends harm, other intercession cannot avail and no one can save the speaker.
It says false gods cannot help their worshippers, directly contradicting reliance on helpers besides God.
It asks whether God is not sufficient for His servant while exposing fear of those invoked besides Him.
It challenges whether those invoked besides God could remove harm He wills or withhold His mercy.
It assigns all intercession to God and His dominion over heaven and earth, limiting every claimed avenue of rescue.
It describes calling on beings besides God that cannot answer, a broader critique of misplaced appeal.
